The Mexican national soccer team had just won a match against Croatia in the World Cup. This meant that Mexico advanced to the next round. Mexican soccer fans worldwide are known for loyalty to their team. After this win, some wonder if they took their loyalty too far.
In Huntington Park, California, fans took to the street after the win. The afternoon crowd grew to almost 200 people. The fans waved flags, yelled, honked their cars, and jumped around the streets. The crowd was so big that they blocked traffic. This caused traffic jams in the area. While most of these fans were just overzealous, a handful were intoxicated. Instead of just celebrating, they began throwing bottles. Some of the fans even began rocking cars parked on the streets. Police were called to the scene. Not only did the local police department send in patrol cars, two police helicopters flew overhead and some police on horseback began to try to disperse the crowd. Someone threw a bottle at a police horse. Police urged shop owners to close their businesses. The police arrested five people. Fortunately no one was hurt.
When Mexico played again the following week, police patrolled the streets in advance. This time they were going to be prepared if Mexico won again. Mexico was playing against the Netherlands. The Dutch team won 2-1. Mexican fans in Huntington Park still took to the streets despite the loss. This time the police were waiting in riot gear. The fans waved flags, chanted, honked horns, rocked cars and even lit firecrackers but no one threw bottles. The police didn't arrest anyone. They did have to close off three blocks to traffic, though. The police were probably secretly glad that Mexico didn't win. In four years, when the next World Cup happens, they'll worry about it again.

**1. Historical and Cultural Origins:**
- **Historical Background:** The origins of Valentine's Day trace back to ancient Roman times with a festival called Lupercalia, which was associated with fertility rites in mid-February. Later, the holiday became linked to Saint Valentine, who is remembered for performing secret marriages during Emperor Claudius II’s reign and for sending messages of affection.
  
- **Cultural Evolution:** Over time, especially during the Middle Ages, the association between love and romance became prominent, leading to the exchange of handwritten notes expressing love. This practice evolved into modern-day traditions involving cards and gifts.

**2. Commercial Aspects:**
- Valentine's Day has become highly commercialized in recent decades. The holiday encourages significant consumer spending on flowers, chocolates, jewelry, and greeting cards.
  
- **Advertising Influence:** As the day approaches, advertising increases dramatically, with companies capitalizing on themes of romance to boost sales. This is evident in the widespread use of imagery like hearts, Cupid, and romantic symbols in marketing campaigns.

- **Gift-Giving:** The exchange of gifts such as flowers, chocolates, or jewelry symbolizes affection and appreciation for one's partner or friends.

- The holiday has adapted over time, with many couples choosing non-traditional ways of celebrating, such as volunteering together or having a quiet night in.

Valentine’s Day serves multiple roles in contemporary society. Balancing traditional practices with modern interpretations allows individuals to celebrate the holiday in ways that resonate personally and culturally.

text:
﻿Facebook has lost millions of users per month in its biggest markets, independent data suggests, as alternative social networks attract the attention of those looking for fresh online playgrounds. 
As Facebook prepares to update investors on its performance in the first three months of the year, with analysts forecasting revenues up 36% on last year, studies suggest that its expansion in the US, UK and other major European countries has peaked. In the last month, the world’s largest social network has lost 6m US visitors, a 4% fall, according to analysis firm Socialbakers. In the UK, 1.4m fewer users checked in in March, a fall of 4.5%. The declines are sustained. In the last six months, Facebook has lost nearly 9m monthly visitors in the US and 2m in the UK. 
Users are also switching off in Canada, Spain, France, Germany and Japan, where Facebook has some of its biggest followings. A spokeswoman for Facebook declined to comment. 
“The problem is that, in the US and UK, most people who want to sign up for Facebook have already done it,” said new media specialist Ian Maude at Enders Analysis. “There is a boredom factor where people like to try something new. Is Facebook going to go the way of MySpace? The risk is relatively small, but that is not to say it isn’t there.” Alternative social networks such as Instagram, the photo-sharing site that won 30m users in 18 months before Facebook acquired the business, have seen surges in popularity with younger age groups. 
Path, the mobile phone-based social network founded by former Facebook employee Dave Morin, which restricts its users to 150 friends, is gaining 1m users a week. It has recently topped 9m users, with 500,000 Venezuelans downloading the app in a single weekend. 
Facebook is still growing fast in South America. Monthly visitors in Brazil were up 6% in the last month to 70m, according to Socialbakers, whose information is used by Facebook advertisers. India has seen a 4% rise to 64m – still a fraction of the country’s population, leaving room for further growth. 
But in developed markets, other Facebook trackers are reporting declines. Analysts at Jefferies bank have developed an algorithm that interfaces directly with Facebook software and it “suggests user levels in [the first quarter] may have declined from peak”. 
Jefferies saw global numbers peak at 1.05bn a month in January, before falling by 20m in February. Numbers rose again in April. The network has now lost nearly 2m visitors in the UK since December, according to research firm Nielsen, with its 27m total flat on a year before. 
The number of minutes Americans spend on Facebook appears to be falling, too. The total was 121 billion minutes in December 2012, but that fell to 115 billion minutes in February, according to comScore. 
As Facebook itself has warned, the time spent on its pages from those sitting in front of personal computers is declining rapidly because we are switching our screen time to smartphones and tablets. 
While smartphone minutes have doubled in a year, to 69 a month, that growth is not guaranteed to compensate for dwindling desktop usage. 
Facebook is the most authoritative source on its own user numbers, and the firm will update investors on its performance for the quarter. Wall Street expects revenues of about $1.44bn, up from $1.06bn in 2012. 
Shareholders will be particularly keen to learn how fast Facebook’s mobile user base is growing, and whether advertising revenues are increasing at the same rate. 
Mobile usage represented nearly a quarter of Facebook’s advertising income at the end of 2012, and the network had 680m mobile users a month in December. 
The company warned in recent stockmarket filings that it might be losing “younger users” to “other products and services similar to, or as a substitute for, Facebook”. 
Wary of competition from services that were invented for the mobile phone rather than the PC, founder Mark Zuckerberg has recently driven through a series of new initiatives designed to appeal to smartphone users. The most significant is Facebook Home, software that can be downloaded onto certain Android phones to feed news and photos from friends – and advertising – directly to the owner’s locked home screen.

**U.S. and UK**: Facebook, once the dominant social media platform, has experienced a decline in user engagement and growth in mature markets like the U.S. and the UK. Over six months leading up to this, Facebook lost nearly 9 million users in the U.S. and 2 million in the UK.

**Europe**: Similar trends are evident across Europe, with significant user losses in countries such as Canada, Spain, France, Germany, and Japan. Experts suggest that many users in these regions might be moving toward alternative platforms.

#### Shift Toward Mobile Engagement

One of Facebook's key challenges is the decline in desktop usage as more people shift to mobile devices. While smartphone engagement has doubled compared to a year ago—reaching 69 minutes per month—the loss from desktop could offset this growth, raising concerns about sustaining ad revenue primarily driven by mobile users.

#### Rise of Alternative Platforms

**Instagram**: Owned by Facebook, Instagram is gaining traction among younger demographics as it offers a photo-sharing experience. This platform benefits from the visual content trend and integrates well with Facebook's broader ecosystem.

### Hollywood Attractions

One of the most iconic aspects of Los Angeles is its deep connection to the film industry, primarily centered around Hollywood. This area is synonymous with fame and has become a major tourist destination due to several key landmarks:

- **The Hollywood Sign**: Perched atop the hills in the Santa Monica Mountains, this famous landmark symbolizes LA's status as the entertainment capital of the world. It can be seen from various vantage points across the city.

- **Hollywood Walk of Fame**: Located in downtown Hollywood, this pedestrian thoroughfare features more than 2,500 brass stars embedded in the sidewalks. - **Universal Studios Hollywood**: This theme park and studio tour offers visitors a glimpse into the world of movie-making. It features attractions based on popular films and TV shows, behind-the-scenes tours, live stunt shows, and themed rides.

- **Santa Monica Pier**: This historic pier is one of the city’s most beloved beachfront attractions. - **Parks and Gardens**: LA boasts lush parks like Griffith Observatory, with its stunning views of the Hollywood Sign and downtown skyline. The nearby Griffith Park offers hiking trails and recreational activities.

- **Dining Scene**: Known for its diverse culinary scene, LA presents an array of dining options ranging from street food to high-end restaurants, reflecting the city’s multicultural makeup.

### Conclusion

Los Angeles is a dynamic city that caters to a wide variety of interests. The real estate developer and art lover donated $40 million, half made up from his private art collection, to the Pérez Art Museum Miami, known as PAMM, one of the few major institutions in the United States with a Hispanic name.
That's certainly one way to put Miami on the map.
Ancient village found in Miami
Downtown Miami is in the midst of a major revitalization: David Beckham is hoping to build a stadium there for his recently announced Miami soccer team. Within the art world, the international art and fashion extravaganza Art Basel, which has taken place in Miami Beach for more than a decade, is considered to be the country's leading art fair with 130 international museum and institutions attracting tens of thousands of people to the five-day event.
Jorge Pérez hopes his museum will help take Miami to the next level.
 Cultural institutions have played a critical role in the growth of Miami, with this museum as a leading example, Pérez said in an interview with CNN.
Before Pérez was known as the Condo King of South Florida, he started as an urban planner, focusing on low-income housing developments.
Then, he co-founded a real estate development firm, The Related Group of Florida, working in high-end condo construction in the 1980s.
In 2005, TIME magazine named him one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States.
The 64-year-old billionaire also made Forbes list of 400 richest Americans several times, the only Latino immigrant to do so.
Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before migrating to Miami as a teen. His lifelong passion for Latin American art stems from his upbringing.

I could ride my bike just about any day of the year, and had lots of friends. My best friend was George Kenny. George lived just a few houses down the block from me and we were the same age. Actually, I was about 28 days older than him – a fact that I always threw in his face. "You must respect your elders," I would sometimes tell him. That usually got a nasty response from him. Anyway, George came up to me one day and said, "Hey Richard, why don't we form a bicycle club?"
 
I thought about it for a while, and then he said, "We could give ourselves a cool name and get hats and stickers and have lots of fun. What do you say?"  I immediately fell in love with the idea. "You bet, Georgie Porgy!"  I used to call him that all the time even though I knew he hated it. Well before we knew it, we got a couple of other guys together and came up with the best name for a club ever. We were the "White Skulls."  Why we chose that name, I'll never know, but all the kids seemed to like it, so I was okay with it, too.
The four of us went to the local bike shop and we each picked out a skull decal to put on our bikes. I chose a green one, while Georgie Porgy picked red. He shouted: "I am the red skull! I am the king of the club! If you don't like it, try to take it from me!"  George was a pretty big guy, so no one argued with him. We rode our bikes everywhere and had a great summer. That's how we formed the greatest bike club ever!

***A NEW SEASON OF HORROR IS COMING.***
***Get ready for: FEAR THE WALKING DEAD***

**(Coming This Late Summer)**

---

### 🩸 The Pitch

Before the world collapsed and civilization crumbled, a creeping fear began in the heart of Los Angeles. *Fear The Walking Dead* doesn't just show you survival—it shows you what happens when the monster is staring back from your own reflection. This series takes viewers back to the volatile period immediately before the full-scale outbreak, exploring not only the relentless threat of the infected but the messy, desperate struggle for humanity itself.

### 🏙️ The Setting: Los Angeles
In a sprawling metropolis that thrives on superficial perfection, chaos is waiting just beneath the surface. When the first bites turn routine street life into a nightmare of flesh and blood, families are torn apart, secrets spill out, and the rules of survival change overnight.

### 🔪 Character Spotlight: New Lives in a Dying World

As the world unravels, four lives—bound by proximity and circumstance—are forced to confront the unthinkable.

*   **Sean:** A dedicated teacher thrust into an apocalyptic role he never prepared for. He must protect his students and learn that knowledge is useless when bullets are needed more.
*   **Nancy:** Working within the walls of Sean’s school, Nancy embodies resilience under pressure. Her life—and her family's future—is immediately threatened by the oncoming horror.
*   **The Connection:** The fragile bond between Sean and Nancy deepens into a powerful attraction, forcing them to confront whether love can survive when basic survival is on the line.

**The Family Stakes:**

*   **Nick:** Caught in his mother's orbit, Nick battles internal demons as external forces threaten to shatter his life. His problems become critical obstacles in this brutal new reality.
*   **Ashley:** An ambitious spirit who believes Los Angeles can—and must—move on. Her desire to escape the immediate danger sets her on a volatile path of self-discovery and risk.

### 🚨 What to Expect

***FEAR THE WALKING DEAD*** is an emotional, high-stakes journey into the chaos. It asks: *When the walls fall down, what remains of who you truly are?*

**Mark your calendars.**
***Fear The Walking Dead*** **— Premiering in Late Summer!**

Is Facebook going to go the way of MySpace? The risk is relatively small, but that is not to say it isn’t there.” Alternative social networks such as Instagram, the photo-sharing site that won 30m users in 18 months before Facebook acquired the business, have seen surges in popularity with younger age groups.

India has seen a 4% rise to 64m – still a fraction of the country’s population, leaving room for further growth.

The most significant is Facebook Home, software that can be downloaded onto certain Android phones to feed news and photos from friends – and advertising – directly to the owner’s locked home screen.

The real estate developer and art lover donated $40 million, half made up from his private art collection, to the Pérez Art Museum Miami, known as PAMM, one of the few major institutions in the United States with a Hispanic name.
That's certainly one way to put Miami on the map.
Ancient village found in Miami
Downtown Miami is in the midst of a major revitalization: David Beckham is hoping to build a stadium there for his recently announced Miami soccer team. Within the art world, the international art and fashion extravaganza Art Basel, which has taken place in Miami Beach for more than a decade, is considered to be the country's leading art fair with 130 international museum and institutions attracting tens of thousands of people to the five-day event.
Jorge Pérez hopes his museum will help take Miami to the next level.
 Cultural institutions have played a critical role in the growth of Miami, with this museum as a leading example, Pérez said in an interview with CNN.
Before Pérez was known as the Condo King of South Florida, he started as an urban planner, focusing on low-income housing developments.
Then, he co-founded a real estate development firm, The Related Group of Florida, working in high-end condo construction in the 1980s.
In 2005, TIME magazine named him one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States.
The 64-year-old billionaire also made Forbes list of 400 richest Americans several times, the only Latino immigrant to do so.
Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before migrating to Miami as a teen. His lifelong passion for Latin American art stems from his upbringing.
In his early 20s, he started collecting paintings by Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia. Now, 110 works selected by the museum from Pérez's private collection are available for everyone to see inside the three-story, 200,000-square-foot museum, designed by the Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron.
Walk inside the $220 million building and you will be surrounded by tall glass windows that are said to be the largest hurricane impact resistant in the world. Hanging from every side of the museum are 70 self-watering hydroponic gardens, designed by French landscape artist Patrick Blanc.
The museum focuses on international art of the 20th and 21st centuries, and is currently showing Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei's According to What ? collection.
PAMM is one of the main attractions in what was known as Bicentennial Park, now Museum Park -- which will also house the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science, set to open in 2015.
The Pérez Art Museum had a smooth opening last year except for one slight hiccup: naming it.
While the majority of board members voted in favor of naming the museum after Pérez, four resigned in protest. It seems they had their heart set on the Miami Art Museum. 
That's because $100 million of the $167 million raised was city and county taxpayer money and the city of Miami donated the waterfront land where PAMM sits. Some of the board members argued the name of the museum should represent the city's central art museum.
 I can not speak for others. However, the great majority of the board was supportive. On a board of 47, 43 voted in favor of the renaming, Pérez said.
Pérez has been involved with the museum since well before the building project began and he said he is honored the board chose to recognize him in that way.
 I think most people want to be remembered with the causes they feel worthwhile and helped promote, Pérez said.
It seemed odd that PAMM received its share of strife for naming it after donor when just a few years ago the Miami Science Museum's name was changed to the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science after a generous donor who gave $35 million to construct the new museum in Museum Park.
 The name change has been extremely well received by the community. Patricia and Phillip Frost are very well-liked people and they symbolize what we 're about, said Gillian Thomas, president and CEO of Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science.
When it comes to naming rights, perhaps Miami takes its art more seriously than science.
 People have opinions about art, whereas science is a bit more concrete, so there would n't be backlash for naming a building after a donor, Thomas said.
But, she points out, naming Miami's art museum after Pérez carries a sense of pride for the Hispanic community, even though his art donation does n't represent a collection. 
 Jorge Pérez is the first major donor from the Hispanic community, Thomas said.
Other American art museums have been named after donors, like The J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, and have n't stirred any controversy.
 While people may not agree on a name, Thomas said, everyone can see that downtown Miami is quickly becoming a hub for science and art, which means donations are needed. 
So far that does n't seem to be a problem for the Pérez Art Museum; it has reached the 90 % mark in its $220 million capital campaign.

Pérez, who loves art, donated $40 million to the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). He used money from his own private art collection for half of this donation. PAMM is one of the few major museums in the U.S. with a Hispanic name. This move should help put Miami on the map.

Downtown Miami is undergoing a big transformation, or "revitalization." For example, David Beckham plans to build a new soccer stadium there for his team. When it comes to art, the massive event called Art Basel takes place in Miami Beach every year. It is huge! More than 130 international museums and centers draw tens of thousands of people to this five-day fair.

Jorge Pérez hopes his museum will help lift Miami to the next level. He told CNN that having cultural places is very important for Miami's growth, and PAMM is a great example.

Before he was known as the "Condo King" in South Florida, Pérez started out working as an urban planner who focused on housing for people with low incomes. Later, he co-founded a real estate company, The Related Group of Florida, where he built fancy condos starting in the 1980s.

In 2005, *TIME* magazine named him one of the top 25 most important Hispanic leaders in the United States. He also appeared on Forbes' list of 400 richest Americans multiple times—making him the only Latino immigrant to do so. Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before moving to Miami as a teenager. His deep love for Latin American art comes from his childhood experiences.

In his early twenties, he began collecting paintings by artists like Diego Rivera and Roberto Matta. Now, 110 works selected from Pérez’s collection are available for everyone to see inside the three-story museum. The building is massive—it covers 200,000 square feet—and was designed by famous architects.

Walking inside the $220 million building, you will notice tall glass windows that are meant to resist hurricanes. Hanging from every side of the museum are 70 self-watering gardens, designed by French artist Patrick Blanc.

The museum focuses on international art from the 20th and 21st centuries. It is currently showing artwork from Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei.

PAMM sits in an area called Museum Park. This park will also house a new science museum, set to open later.

Pérez said he felt honored that the board chose to honor him. He believes people want to be remembered for good causes they support.

This argument was strange because not long ago, the Miami Science Museum changed its name after another generous donor who gave $35 million to build the new building in Museum Park. The community welcomed that change very well.

Thomas, the CEO of the science museum, said that when it comes to naming rights, maybe Miami takes art more seriously than science. She also pointed out that while Pérez's art gift is amazing, it doesn't represent a whole collection. Nevertheless, she said that naming the art museum after Pérez shows pride for the Hispanic community.

Other big American art museums have been named after donors without causing trouble. While people may disagree on the name, everyone can see that downtown Miami is quickly becoming an important place for both science and art—and this means more donations are needed.  Without a doubt, he marked the road in this final successful phase. I felt a great deal of appreciation towards him, Del Bosque told the national team's official website.
 I knew he had some health problems, but I never imagined it would lead to this.

 Luis Aragones was a great player and coach, but before all that a great person and a friend, said the team's president Enrique Cerezo.

Miami is renowned for its tropical climate, retiree community, and significant Cuban-American population; however, it's not as well-known internationally as an art hub. Fortunately, billionaire real estate developer Jorge Pérez aims to change this for downtown Miami.

Pérez, a patron of the arts, donated $40 million - half from his personal art collection - to the Perez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), one of few major institutions in the United States with a Hispanic name. This move is certainly a step towards elevating Miami's status on the global art scene.

The city is undergoing significant development, particularly downtown. David Beckham plans to construct a stadium there for his newly announced Miami soccer team. Within the art world, Miami Beach has been hosting Art Basel - considered America's leading art fair - for over a decade, attracting tens of thousands of people during its five-day event.

Jorge Pérez believes that his museum will further propel Miami into prominence. He stated in an interview with CNN that cultural institutions like this one have played a critical role in the growth of Miami.

Before becoming known as the Condo King of South Florida, Pérez began as an urban planner, focusing on low-income housing developments. Subsequently, he co-founded a real estate development firm, The Related Group of Florida, engaging in high-end condo construction during the 1980s.

In 2005, TIME magazine recognized Pérez as one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States. He has been listed several times on Forbes' list of 400 richest Americans - the only Latino immigrant to achieve this distinction. Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before relocating to Miami as a teenager. His lifelong love for Latin American art stemmed from his upbringing.

In his twenties, Pérez started amassing paintings by artists such as Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia. Now, 110 pieces selected by the museum from Pérez's private collection are on display within the three-story, 200,000 square-foot building, designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron.

Since $100 million of the raised $167 million was city and county taxpayer money, some board members believed that the name should reflect Miami's central art museum. Despite this controversy, Pérez has been involved with the museum since its inception and expressed honor at being recognized in such a way.

Downtown Miami is currently undergoing significant revitalization. David Beckham plans to build a stadium there for his newly announced Miami soccer team, and the city plays host to Art Basel, the country's leading art fair, which attracts tens of thousands of people during its five-day event in Miami Beach.

Jorge Pérez hopes that his museum will contribute to taking Miami to the next level within the art world. In an interview with CNN, he stated that cultural institutions have played a critical role in the city's growth, with PAMM as a prime example. Before becoming known as the Condo King of South Florida, Pérez began his career as an urban planner, focusing on low-income housing developments. He later co-founded The Related Group of Florida and worked in high-end condo construction during the 1980s.

Pérez has been recognized for his achievements, earning a spot on TIME magazine's list of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States in 2005. He has also appeared multiple times on Forbes' list of 400 richest Americans, making him the only Latino immigrant to do so.

Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before moving to Miami as a teenager. His lifelong passion for Latin American art can be traced back to his upbringing. In his early twenties, he began collecting paintings by Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia. Now, 110 works selected from Pérez's private collection are on display inside the three-story, 200,000-square-foot museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron.

The $220 million building features tall glass windows said to be the largest hurricane impact resistant in the world and 70 self-watering hydroponic gardens designed by French landscape artist Patrick Blanc. The museum focuses on international art of the 20th and 21st centuries, currently showcasing Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei's According to What? collection.

PAMM is one of the main attractions in Museum Park, which will also house the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science, set to open in 2015. The museum faced a slight controversy during its naming process; while the majority of board members voted in favor of naming it after Pérez, four resigned in protest due to the city's central art museum traditionally being named as such. text:
﻿Facebook has lost millions of users per month in its biggest markets, independent data suggests, as alternative social networks attract the attention of those looking for fresh online playgrounds. 
As Facebook prepares to update investors on its performance in the first three months of the year, with analysts forecasting revenues up 36% on last year, studies suggest that its expansion in the US, UK and other major European countries has peaked. In the last month, the world’s largest social network has lost 6m US visitors, a 4% fall, according to analysis firm Socialbakers. In the UK, 1.4m fewer users checked in in March, a fall of 4.5%. The declines are sustained. In the last six months, Facebook has lost nearly 9m monthly visitors in the US and 2m in the UK. 
Users are also switching off in Canada, Spain, France, Germany and Japan, where Facebook has some of its biggest followings. A spokeswoman for Facebook declined to comment. 
“The problem is that, in the US and UK, most people who want to sign up for Facebook have already done it,” said new media specialist Ian Maude at Enders Analysis. “There is a boredom factor where people like to try something new. Is Facebook going to go the way of MySpace? The risk is relatively small, but that is not to say it isn’t there.” Alternative social networks such as Instagram, the photo-sharing site that won 30m users in 18 months before Facebook acquired the business, have seen surges in popularity with younger age groups. 
Path, the mobile phone-based social network founded by former Facebook employee Dave Morin, which restricts its users to 150 friends, is gaining 1m users a week. It has recently topped 9m users, with 500,000 Venezuelans downloading the app in a single weekend. 
Facebook is still growing fast in South America. Monthly visitors in Brazil were up 6% in the last month to 70m, according to Socialbakers, whose information is used by Facebook advertisers.  Cultural institutions have played a critical role in the growth of Miami, with this museum as a leading example, Pérez said in an interview with CNN.

 While people may not agree on a name, Thomas said, everyone can see that downtown Miami is quickly becoming a hub for science and art, which means donations are needed. 
So far that does n't seem to be a problem for the Pérez Art Museum; it has reached the 90 % mark in its $220 million capital campaign.

text:
﻿Facebook has lost millions of users per month in its biggest markets, independent data suggests, as alternative social networks attract the attention of those looking for fresh online playgrounds. 
As Facebook prepares to update investors on its performance in the first three months of the year, with analysts forecasting revenues up 36% on last year, studies suggest that its expansion in the US, UK and other major European countries has peaked. In the last month, the world’s largest social network has lost 6m US visitors, a 4% fall, according to analysis firm Socialbakers. In the UK, 1.4m fewer users checked in in March, a fall of 4.5%. The declines are sustained. In the last six months, Facebook has lost nearly 9m monthly visitors in the US and 2m in the UK. 
Users are also switching off in Canada, Spain, France, Germany and Japan, where Facebook has some of its biggest followings. A spokeswoman for Facebook declined to comment. 
“The problem is that, in the US and UK, most people who want to sign up for Facebook have already done it,” said new media specialist Ian Maude at Enders Analysis. “There is a boredom factor where people like to try something new. Is Facebook going to go the way of MySpace? The risk is relatively small, but that is not to say it isn’t there.” Alternative social networks such as Instagram, the photo-sharing site that won 30m users in 18 months before Facebook acquired the business, have seen surges in popularity with younger age groups. 
Path, the mobile phone-based social network founded by former Facebook employee Dave Morin, which restricts its users to 150 friends, is gaining 1m users a week. It has recently topped 9m users, with 500,000 Venezuelans downloading the app in a single weekend. 
Facebook is still growing fast in South America. Monthly visitors in Brazil were up 6% in the last month to 70m, according to Socialbakers, whose information is used by Facebook advertisers. India has seen a 4% rise to 64m – still a fraction of the country’s population, leaving room for further growth. 
But in developed markets, other Facebook trackers are reporting declines. Analysts at Jefferies bank have developed an algorithm that interfaces directly with Facebook software and it “suggests user levels in [the first quarter] may have declined from peak”. 
Jefferies saw global numbers peak at 1.05bn a month in January, before falling by 20m in February. Numbers rose again in April. The network has now lost nearly 2m visitors in the UK since December, according to research firm Nielsen, with its 27m total flat on a year before. 
The number of minutes Americans spend on Facebook appears to be falling, too. The total was 121 billion minutes in December 2012, but that fell to 115 billion minutes in February, according to comScore. 
As Facebook itself has warned, the time spent on its pages from those sitting in front of personal computers is declining rapidly because we are switching our screen time to smartphones and tablets. 
While smartphone minutes have doubled in a year, to 69 a month, that growth is not guaranteed to compensate for dwindling desktop usage. 
Facebook is the most authoritative source on its own user numbers, and the firm will update investors on its performance for the quarter. Wall Street expects revenues of about $1.44bn, up from $1.06bn in 2012. 
Shareholders will be particularly keen to learn how fast Facebook’s mobile user base is growing, and whether advertising revenues are increasing at the same rate. 
Mobile usage represented nearly a quarter of Facebook’s advertising income at the end of 2012, and the network had 680m mobile users a month in December. 
The company warned in recent stockmarket filings that it might be losing “younger users” to “other products and services similar to, or as a substitute for, Facebook”. 
Wary of competition from services that were invented for the mobile phone rather than the PC, founder Mark Zuckerberg has recently driven through a series of new initiatives designed to appeal to smartphone users. The most significant is Facebook Home, software that can be downloaded onto certain Android phones to feed news and photos from friends – and advertising – directly to the owner’s locked home screen.
